speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-ANSWER TO STARRED QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege that affects the rights and prerogatives of the House of Commons. I hope the Prime Minister, as the custodian of those rights under your direction, sir, will join with me in what I am about to say. I refer to an answer in Hansard as reported at page 13065. The material portion of the question I asked was this:
What are the names and addresses of the chosen officials and/or employees of the C.B.C. who are to be the recipients of and have free use of the coloured T.V. sets recently purchased by the C.B.C.
You will recall, sir, that the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek first brought this matter to the light of day. Yesterday the answer was given by the minister and, of course, she only transmits that which is given to her by the corporation. The answer to that question which was worded in such a way that there would be no ambiguity, was:
Colour television receivers are assigned according to requirements of senior positions and remain with these positions in the event of the departure of present incumbents. They are used by those whose duties require program viewing.
Sir, that answer took several weeks in incubation. It was delayed for days on end until I rose on a question of privilege. That answer indicates a cavalier contempt of parliament. The C.B.C. secures the major portion of its income from the people of Canada, and parliament is not secondary to the C.B.C. The question was allowed, it was on the order paper, and parliament's right to obtain this information has not been challenged.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I rise at this time simply to ask for an answer. The answer may be embarrassing to some who have become voluntary recipients of the public benevolence at the expense of the people of Canada, but whatever may be the embarrassment the answer must be given. Unless the answer is given in a satisfactory
way early next week it will become necessary in the interests of preserving the rights of parliament to take such action as the traditions and prerogatives of parliament permit. I hope that will not be necessary.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, February 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Sharp for the second reading of Bill No. C-268, to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Old Age Security Act, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Knowles.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I should like to take a few minutes to complete the remarks I was making yesterday when we adjourned.
It seems to me that in introducing this bill the Minister of Finance, is doing precisely, in respect of people in lower income brackets and on fixed incomes such as pension allowances of various kinds, that which he warned us about some months ago. He has been warning us since last spring that we are facing a spiralling inflation and an ever increasing and alarming cost of living.
Some time ago the minister suggested that we must exercise care in order to stop or slow down this increasing cost of living, yet what he is proposing by this bill will inevitably have the result of increasing the cost of living for those people who can least afford it, the people on fixed incomes and in the low income brackets, whether they work for wages or derive their livelihood from farming. As was pointed out yesterday, the 1 per cent increase in sales tax applied at the manufacturers' level will increase as it is passed on from the manufacturer to the wholesaler, then to the retailer and finally to the consumer. It has been estimated that this increase will amount to about another 1 per cent, making the total increase to the consumer 2 per cent.
We have heard evidence to the effect that the cost of prescription drugs has gone up by not 1 per cent but 10 per cent or 15 per cent. It must be remembered that this has placed an extra burden on the older people. This has a disastrous effect so far as they are concerned, because generally speaking they need prescription drugs more than others.
Yesterday the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance and another parliamentary secretary invited us to suggest an alternative way of raising funds to cover the increases in old age pensions. I suggested an alternative yesterday. I do not have the facilities to work out whether my alternative would provide as much money as the 1 per cent increase in sales tax.
Excise Tax and Old Age Security Act
For many years we have followed the principle of a graduated and progressive income tax policy under which people who earn the most money pay the highest income taxes, and pay them at higher percentage rates. I think most members of this house and most people in this country believe in this principle. That being so, it is completely wrong for this government to suggest that taxpayers should pay 4 per cent of their income with a limit of $240 per year toward the old age security fund. As I said yesterday in answer to the parliamentary secretary, it is much easier for every member of parliament and every businessman in this country who has a taxable income of $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000 to pay the 4 per cent increase than it is for those on fixed or low incomes to pay the 1 per cent increase in sales tax.
Because I believe this proposal is inherently unjust, and because I believe those in the upper income brackets are not being asked to pay their fair share, I have no hesitation in supporting the amendment moved by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and in effect voting against the proposal incorporated in this bill which will impose a substantial increase in the taxes of the people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, nothing would have pleased the Minister of Finance more than to have avoided increasing taxes to meet the costs of the guaranteed income plan for old age pensioners, and it might even have made the Minister of Finance much more popular. But as Minister of Finance I have a responsibility to be, not popular but, in so far as possible, wise. Sometimes I may succeed, sometimes I may not, but at any rate it is incumbent upon me as Minister of Finance to be concerned about the interests of all Canadians, and particularly to ensure that steady kind of economic progress that is vital to everyone in this country and particularly to the workers and farmers.
13110	COMMONS
Excise Tax and Old Age Security Act
If one looks at the history of governments in the world over the centuries I think one is forced to conclude that it is because governments from time to time have not been prepared to face up to their responsibilities that in the world at large over the centuries we have had too much inflation. The problem we face in the world today in relation to economic expansion is to try to create conditions in which we have steady economic expansion without inflation. No country in the world has ever succeeded in this. Too often in the past we have had a boom and bust type of economy. If one wanted to look around the world for an example of the serious problems that arise when not enough attention is given to this situation, one has only to look at the United Kingdom today, where because of the failure to deal adequately with the problem of ensuring steady expansion without inflation the government of that country is forced to the kind of measures that I sometimes think our friends in the N.D.P. are now advocating.
Mr. Speaker, if there had been any prospect whatever that there would be surplus revenues either during this fiscal year or during any subsequent fiscal year out of which we could have met these large additions to our expenditures, which I hope everyone in this house supports fully, I might have made different recommendations on this occasion. The government, looking at prospects, came to the conclusion that there was no prospect whatever that out of existing revenues we could meet the costs of the guaranteed income plan plus the other obligations the government faces and that have been supported on all sides of this house, as we have introduced legislation and as we have introduced estimates. The government therefore considered it wise on this occasion to avoid adding to any prospective deficit by raising immediately the large sums required for the supplement to old age pensions.
Much has been made of the fact that part of the revenues has been put into the old age security fund and part has gone into general revenues. In my address to the house on December 19 when I introduced these proposals I made quite clear what we were doing and why we were doing it, and I certainly resent any of the suggestions that have been made that at any time I misled the house or the public as to what we were doing.
May I, for the benefit of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who I am sure will continue to make these

DEBATES	February 16, 1967
points regardless of what I say, and for the record refer again to what I said about the old age security fund. I said on December 19, as reported at page 11334 of Hansard:
When we consider the economic and financial effects of old age security payments, however, we must look not to the position in a single account but to total cash flows. In introducing the guaranteed income supplement we are adding $280 million a year to our cash outflow, and this must somehow be matched by increased cash revenues if we are to avoid increasing our cash deficit with all its financial and economic consequences. The accumulated surplus of the old age security account is not held in a separate cash balance. The cash received and credited to this account is and always has been pooled in the consolidated revenue fund into which parliament requires all revenues to be paid and from which the payments authorized by parliament are made.
This is the situation, Mr. Speaker. It has always been this way. If I thought I had some cash or some revenue that I could substitute for moneys borrowed or moneys raised by taxation, I would certainly have taken a different course. But in fact our expenditures are going up by $280 million, and I feel it wise under these circumstances to raise $280 million, approximately, for this purpose.

I will refer to a few of the suggestions for immediate action which have been made by the N.D.P. in the house and I want to stress the point that these proposals have been made for immediate action, not for action in the future. Indeed, on many occasions they have gone out of their way to castigate the government for not embarking immediately upon these expenditure programs, the most important of which is the one that I first mentioned. They have criticized the government for not paying $105 a month to all recipients of old age security. They have also proposed the abolition of university fees. Excise Tax and Old Age Security Act some of the measures that the N.D.P. would wish to implement immediately, would be equivalent to about 8 percentage points in the sales tax and would amount to about half of the revenues of our existing personal income taxes. These are the sort of tax changes which the N.D.P. is advocating immediately, I understand, and yet they are proposing that we should hoist for six months a bill which advocates an increase in tax not of $1,200 million but of $280 million.
I should like to speak now about the sales tax increase which is the point that led the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to propose the six months hoist. In supporting this amendment the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Mac-Innis) said the following yesterday, as reported on page 13094 of Hansard:
We feel very strongly that this type of tax should not be imposed as a means of helping people in the old age pension group because at the same time we say we are helping them we are making things more difficult for them by increasing the sales tax.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), however, took a rather different line and under some pressure from this side of the house admitted that he felt there might be some virtue in a sales tax but he thought it should be in the form of a retail sales tax rather than a manufacturers' sales tax. This is a problem in taxation which has concerned tax experts for a long time and there are arguments on both sides. As I see it, the position taken by the N.D.P. on this question is partly represented by the view taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who does not like this tax at all because somehow he feels it is not right for us to impose taxes to cover the full amount of the cost. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway does not like it either because it has certain economic effects and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni does not like the manufacturers' tax and would prefer a retail sales tax. Perhaps the reason why members of that party are prepared to support this amendment is that they managed to find some common ground upon which they can agree.
However, as I was listening to the debate I asked one of the hon. members who was speaking whether he was equally opposed to provincial sales taxes, to which he said yes. I asked him whether he was also opposed to the sales tax in Saskatchewan and he said yes. I then took a good look at the history of the sales tax in Saskatchewan and

DEBATES	February 16, 1967
I would like to give a brief recital of the facts. In 1937, following a recommendation of a royal commission headed by Mr. Neil Jacoby, a retail sales tax was introduced at 2 per cent and it was called an education tax. The proceeds from this tax were used exclusively for educational purposes. In 1944 the C.C.F. government came to office under the premiership of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and in 1950 the tax was renamed the education and hospitalization tax and was increased to 3 per cent. In 1962 the tax was given another name which related more closely to the purpose for which it was to be raised and was called the education and health tax. At that time it was increased to 5 per cent and 50 per cent of the revenues were to be used for education, 30 per cent for hospitalization and 20 per cent for medical care.
Here we have the leader of a party in this house, who as premier of a province at one time imposed a 5 per cent sales tax for education, hospitalization and medical care, now supporting an amendment in the house implying that a 1 per cent increase in the manufacturers' sales tax is iniquitous and is somehow working to the detriment of those whom we are trying to help. Perhaps the hon. member has a convenient memory and will argue that at that time special circumstances prevailed. I suggest that those decisions were taken because he believed that this was a reasonable way of raising the revenues he needed.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Following that, indeed, in confirmation of it, Mr. Speaker, a royal commission on taxation in the province of Saskatchewan was appointed in 1963. I should like to read a paragraph or two of that report about the economics of such a tax. At page 162 of the report of the royal commission on taxation, province of Saskatchewan, 1965, there appears this paragraph:
The views which we express concerning the retail sales tax are not based only upon its current apparent acceptability-although acceptability or lack of it is certainly a matter of considerable importance in determining the usefulness of any tax form. We have concluded that a properly structured retail sales tax is a "fair" mode of taxation in that it does distribute its burdens according to at least one reasonably adequate measure of income-actual expenditures on consumption. Moreover, to the extent that expenditures on certain basic necessities of life-for example, food and shelter-are exempted from the operations of the tax, then low income groups are relieved of its most burdensome aspects, and it may be levied in accordance with reasonable concepts of ability to pay.

That is a judgment rendered upon the tax structure of Saskatchewan in which the retail sales tax is very substantial. I believe that it does support the reasonableness under modem conditions, of raising part of the needed revenues by a tax on consumption. The report also points out and reinforces the argument I made in my address on December 19, that if one does impose a manufacturers' or sales tax and exempts food, fuel and shelter one arrives at a tax that bears at least some relationship to ability to pay and is certainly not regressive.

People would see a relationship between contributions to the fund and the amount of the pension. It did not work that way. I believe the old age security fund has outlived its usefulness and I am in a mood to consider a change. A good deal, of course, depends upon the sort of recommendations we get for revision of our tax system as a whole. In the meantime, however, I believe we ought to maintain the principle of the old age security fund, that is, that there should be some relationship between the amount of contributions from personal income and the amount of benefit. If one looks back in history one will find that when the tax was first imposed in 1952 there was a 2 per cent tax on incomes with a maximum of $60, in 1959 a 3 per cent with the maximum raised to $90, and in 1964 the rate on personal income was raised to 4 per cent and the maximum to $120. When a municipality, a province or a country is in need of money, bonds are offered for sale; the party with empty coffers has become a vendor. With this approach, it is not surprising if certain newspapers have referred to the tax increase then presented by the government as a gift.

Mr. Chairman, I was very interested in the remarks of the Minister of Finance this afternoon. I was rather impressed by the sweet reasonableness of his approach in examining the proposals of the

New Democratic Party. He seemed to indicate that he agreed in principle with many of our objectives and that he and other members of his party were in favour of increasing foreign aid and believe in research, education and the need to make university education available to those who could benefit, and medicare, but that it was with profound regret he had to step in and tell the government that his judgment indicated that the government could not afford these things. He also expressed his deep sympathy that the aspirations of the older people of this country who need increased pensions could not be met.
The minister mentioned an estimated cost of $900 million in respect of these programs. It is not my intention to quarrel with that figure because it is not particularly important now. No one questions the fact that these programs would require substantial expenditures. No one will argue that these programs could be carried out without incurring expenditures. However, the minister seems to ignore a number of aspects involved in this kind of situation. He seems to ignore the fact that many of these programs can be considered as investments in Canada's future. When people spend to increase the potential and the productivity of the nation the whole situation takes on a different light. One cannot believe that these programs involve merely an outflow without any return. There has been evidence in respect of foreign aid that frequently the aid giving nation over a period of time obtains very substantial benefits in increased trade, good will and access to markets. Research and investment are important to a nation attempting to achieve growth.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
If we consider the remarks of the Economic Council pointing out the lower level of expenditure on education in Canada and the lower attainment of education at the post-secondary level, we have to question whether we can really defer programs of this kind on the argument that we cannot afford them. It seems to many of us that the one thing we cannot afford to do is to ignore the important aspects of these expenditures vis-a-vis the long-run future of the country.
The minister, as I said, was being reasonable in his approach. He was almost professorial, indicating that he had considerable regret in coming before the house and pointing out that the money just was not there for these purposes and therefore we had to accept the proposition he was putting forward. The difficulty in accepting what the minister says
February 16. 1967	COMMONS
in this regard is that he gave us no indication that there are other ways of increasing government revenues without necessarily increasing tax rates.
We all know there is a limit on the amount of taxation people are prepared to accept. But there is an important way of increasing government revenues that the minister has not touched upon that is, the outstanding requirement in this country to increase our level of productivity and the wealth base from which the costs of the social service, scientific and foreign aid programs can be met. We have had a rather dismal record in this country in terms of increasing our productivity. If we refer to a table on page 16 of the third annual review of the Economic Council of Canada which shows the growth of productivity from 1955 to 1965, we see that Canada is 14th in the list of industrialized nations. We have had one of the lowest rates of productivity increase of almost any of the industrialized countries of the world. When we look at these figures and recognize that many of these countries which have a much higher productivity growth rate than Canada spend considerably more than this country in the fields of social welfare, research and foreign aid, we realize that for the minister to come before this house and say "I would love to do all these things but we simply cannot afford it" is to beg the question completely.
Surely the real problem facing the minister is to see that his government brings in programs that will enable this nation to fulfil its obligations and find its proper place in the sun, instead of wringing his hands at the prospect of programs which even he admits are desirable but says we cannot afford. Canada, according to the Economic Council and according to almost any observer who has looked at our economy, is potentially the wealthiest nation in the world. We have in this country almost everything that any nation could hope to have if it is looking for wealth. I think there is general agreement about that. Despite the enormous potentiality in this country our productivity is approximately 25 per cent lower than that of other industrialized nations. The figures vary between 20 per cent and 30 per cent. We have to ask ourselves the question: Why should this be? If we talk about capital investment in this country and say that we urgently need tremendous quantities of capital in order to improve our productivity, this is very true.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I shall speak briefly and deal in broad terms with the provisions of this bill. I am hopeful hon. members will feel at the conclusion of this hour that the bill be given second reading, after which it will be referred to the standing committee on transport and communications. I would be surprised if hon. members did not wish to deal in more detail with certain portions of the bill and to hear the officials of the Bell Telephone Company and other witnesses. I hope hon. members will agree with me that this can be done best in the committee on transport and communications.
In moving second reading of the bill I might mention that its objectives may be classified under four separate heads: First, an amendment affecting the corporate name of the company; second, amendments affecting the capital structure of the company; third, an updating of the corporate powers and, fourth and last, procedural and mechanical amendments.
Over the years the company has become known as Bell Canada. In February, 1956 it obtained permission to use Bell Canada as a trade name. Bell Canada has been used extensively in advertising and other material.

The second group of amendments deals with the capital structure of the company. The company's original act of incorporation dates back to 1880. Over the years, as and when new capital was required, the company applied for increased capital authorizations, and this is a further application before parliament at this time.
During the last decade the Bell Telephone Company of Canada has embarked on a construction program which has required the investment of substantial amounts of both equity and debt money. According to the company's estimate the authorized capital will be virtually exhausted by 1968. If this were to happen before the company receives additional authority to increase its capital, a slow down of the construction program would immediately occur with an instant impact on the Canadian economy. It must be borne in mind that the company currently spends $300 million a year on its construction program which is designed to meet growth and to give its customers improved services such as automatic dialing and so on.
If service is to be maintained, the company needs the authority to issue additional stock. At present 40 million shares of a par value of $25 each have been authorized. Over 34 million shares, of which 94.6 per cent are held in Canada, have already been issued and the employees of the company subscribe from year to year more than $22 million a year.
The increase of $750 million for which approval is now being sought is consistent with the pattern which has developed over the last decade. The company comes before parliament every 9 or 10 years to obtain additional capital authorizations. According to present forecasts the sum of $750 million sought at this time should last approximately ten years.
The company also seeks an amendment to have the power to issue preferred stock whenever conditions warrant such a decision. At present the financing of the company is done exclusively by means of common shares and bonds. There are periods when market conditions could make the issue of preferred stock less burdensome upon the subscribers. In order to have more flexibility and thereby finance the company at reduced cost the company requests an amendment authorizing it to issue preferred shares as and when it might be advantageous for the company to do so. The creation and issue of preferred stock would be subject to the procedure outlined in clause 3 of the bill, which is similar in terms to previous authorizations given by this house to
February 16, 1967

other corporations incorporated by special act.
The company further requests an amendment to its charter allowing it to issue its capital stock without the approval of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. I might mention that any issue of the capital stock of the company is presently subject to the approval of the Board of Transport Commissioners. The board allowed until May, 1966 a permissive level of earnings in terms of dollars per share. In May, 1966 the board changed the basis of the regulation and stated that rates generating a rate of return not exceeding 6.6 per cent on the total invested capital were just and reasonable.
The third group of amendments deals with the updating of the corporate powers of the company. It was recognized by this house when it amended the Criminal Code that the expression "telephone communications" was much too narrow to describe adequately the field of communications. Everyone is now referring to telecommunications, which is a broader term than telephone communications. This is the purpose of clause 7 of the bill.
The company has the corporate power to own, maintain and operate a telephone company and to manufacture electrical equipment. It also has the power to invest in any company possessing as proprietor any line of telephonic or telegraphic communications or in any company possessing the power or right to use communications by means of the telephone. These powers are specified in clauses 2 and 4 of the incorporating statute as amended.
Section 14 (e) of the Canada Corporation Act gives to letters patent companies the ancillary power to invest in companies having objects in whole or in part similar to those of the company. The purpose of clause 8 of the bill is to give Bell Canada similar powers. Clause 8 also seeks to authorize Bell Canada to invest in companies engaged in research and development work. The need for Canadian research is important to our economic progress.
The company also wishes to introduce two social measures to help its employees. Permission to lend money to employees who are in financial difficulties, even if they are shareholders of the company, is requested under clause 12 of the bill. Clause 13 seeks authority to establish a housing plan to assist employees who are transferred in the course of their employment from one area to another.
Private Bills
The other provisions of the bill are procedural or mechanical in character and can be considered as housekeeping matters. I have in mind the clarification of the power of the company to sell shares for cash and to its shareholders, clause 5, the clarification of the number of authorities to be given by the shareholders for borrowing money, clause 6, or other matters dealing with indemnification given to the directors in suits respecting execution of office, clause 10. The record date for meetings, dealt with in clause 15, also falls in this category of housekeeping provisions.
The company also requests authority to create an executive committee to deal with matters delegated to it by the board of directors. In view of the size of the board of directors and the importance of the matters to be transacted at board meetings, the formation of an executive committee with executive powers becomes more and more important for the smooth operation of the business.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
That is all the time I want to take, Mr. Speaker, because I want to give ample time to representatives of the other groups. May I reiterate that I hope we may give the bill second reading today so that we may deal with it in detail in the standing committee.

subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the brief summary of the bill's provisions given by the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Honey) indicated, the bill before the house, even though it is a private member's bill, is in our opinion an extremely important one and should not be passed without very thorough study by the appropriate committee. Indeed, as far as we are concerned we could not possibly support the bill in its present form.
What this bill does, if I may summarize it in my own way, is to seek to extend the field of the Bell Telephone Company almost without limit into the entire area of telecommunications. It seeks to extend its field into the broadcasting area. It seeks to give the Bell Telephone Company powers for very widespread vertical integration by giving it authority to acquire companies without limiting it any longer to those which have or use telephone lines, as was the case formerly. Clause 8 of the bill provides that the company can extend its operations, its purchases and acquisitions very widely, so it is obvious the company can use that power to build an empire of satellite activities, industrial and commercial, almost without limit. Under the bill

February 16, 1967
Private Bills
the Bell Telephone Company seeks to get away in part from the regulations to which it is now subject under the Board of Transport Commissioners. Its rates would still be subject to regulation but the issuance of shares would no longer be subject to any investigation or inquiry by the board. The bill seeks to increase the capitalization of the company from $1 billion to $lf billion, which would give it a tremendous base for financial development of a huge size.
Before we do that, Mr. Speaker, we ought to know a great many things about the intentions of the company. I am sure we ought to investigate rather carefully how the company has so far used the powers it has had. If any company has enjoyed a monopoly in its services, this company has. It has almost a complete monopoly in Canada or in the major parts of this country.
The company has had tremendous earnings, Mr. Speaker, and I think some information in this regard ought to be put on the record to show what the company has enjoyed as a result of the incorporation it received in 1880 and the various amendments which have been made since. Since the end of the last war the operating revenues of the company increased from $77 million in 1946 to about $593 million in 1965. The 1965 report of the company, which I have before me, gives the first nine months of 1966 and if you project those nine months to a full 12 month period the gross operating revenue of the company amounted to $638 million last year. The operating revenues, therefore, have increased nine times in the 20 years from 1946 to 1966.
So far as net income is concerned, it was $8 million in 1946 and increased to $861,- million in 1965. A projection on the same basis I have mentioned indicates that the net income for 1966 probably was around $88 million or an increase of 11 times in 20 years.
It is interesting in these statistics to note the effect of automation and how these huge increases in operating revenues and net earnings took place in relation to the work force. I have the figures only from 1959 on in the report which, as I have said before, is in front of me. From 1959 to 1965 operating revenues increased by 57J per cent and net income increased by over 71 per cent. The work force, however, increased by only 3 per cent in those seven years. An increase of 3 per cent in the number of employees enabled the company to increase its operating revenues by 57i per cent and its net income by over 71 per cent.

We ought to make a careful study to see what the company has done for the people of Canada to deserve this tremendous growth in revenues and profits. How has it treated its Canadian subscribers? According to some of the evidence given before the Board of Transport Commissioners-I cannot say whether the evidence is accurate but so far as I have been able to find out it has not been contradicted-the company has increased rates over the years to Canadian subscribers by making earnings which for a number of years exceeded the level of earnings the Board of Transport Commissioners permitted. During those years when the permissive level of earnings was based on so many dollars on a certain value of shares. For years, therefore, the company, so far as I have been able to find out, deliberately violated the instructions given by the body set up by this parliament with authority to give those orders, and the company increased the rates to subscribers in order to help it violate those instructions. We ought to know about that. We ought to know whether the consumers of telephone services in Canada have been treated shabbily by this company before we give it these extra powers.
As a result of my study of this material, Mr. Speaker, I would say the company has not taken the national interest into account or the interest of the subscribers to its service. We ought to know, exactly what is the relationship of this company to its subsidiaries. This report tells me there are 16 subsidiaries of the Bell Telephone Company, some of them wholly owned and some of them subsidiaries of subsidiaries. When I see that I am concerned about the additional powers the company wants under clause 8 of the bill which would enable it to go still further afield.
We have the usual consolidated statements, the usual refusal of the parent company to give information, even to the Board of Transport Commissioners, about the precise relationship between Northern Electric and the Bell Telephone Company. There are the usual suspicions, usually well grounded, that the Northern Electric Company sells its products to the parent company at a price which is unnecessarily high for intercompany reasons that have nothing to do with the national interest. There is the usual secrecy about precisely what Northern Electric is doing, how much it is making, and a lot of other relevant information is also denied us.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
I was interested to find that this matter has concerned governments over the years, Mr. February 16, 1967

Speaker, and I should like to put on record, because I think it is both relevant and illuminating, an extract taken from a brief which was presented to the Board of Transport Commissioners in 1926, when the Bell Company asked for a rate increase, by the Conservative government of Premier Ferguson of the province of Ontario. This is what the brief says in part:
Reference in this connection might also be made to the covering up and the scurrying-to-cover tactics in connection with the disclosure of all relations and dealings of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada and its subsidiary the Northern Electric Manufacturing Company-
As it was then called.
-which latter company is merely the directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, and the Bell Telephone Company itself manufacturing apparatus and selling it to themselves under another name at high monopoly prices, fixed and agreed upon between each company and its directors thereby making it possible to empty the Bell treasury and create a deficit when a rate case is coming, or at any time it sees fit to do so.
That is the statement that was made by the government of Ontario in 1926. I cannot say whether that statement would still apply in its entirety, but I have no hesitation in expressing the opinion, based on some years of trying to understand operations of this sort, that the prices which the Northern Electric Company charges Bell do not necessarily have any relationship to the market price or cost of the products allegedly sold to Bell. Indeed, they have a relationship to the financial arrangements between these two companies and the eventual financial statement of the Bell Telephone Company itself.
The Ferguson government brief to which I have just referred contains a statement couched in stronger language than I would use but which is perhaps perfectly legitimate language. It stated:
This is the most barefaced piece of villainy and imposition ever attempted upon a free people ... and its exposure before this honourable board will not be the last this corporate monopoly will hear about it.
I do not want it to be the last, Mr. Speaker. I think that all these matters should be carefully inquired into by the appropriate committee of this house. I want to know what is the exact effect of the relationship between Bell and the American Telephone and Telegraph Company. I know that the Bell Company boasts of the fact that 94 per cent of its shares, or some such percentage, are owned in Canada by some 240,000 shareholders. I think that is the number published in their report and prospectus. If they say so then I have no
Private Bills
doubt that their share books will show it. But there has been more than one occasion in our kind of economy when a company which has owned as A.T.&T. does, 2.2 per cent of shares has been in a position to exercise control.
I should like to know, and I am sure the house would, to what extent Bell is at the service of A.T.&T. I want to know whether the service contract between Bell and the American Company, which enables Bell to use certain of A.T.&T. developments in Canada but gives the American company the top 1 per cent of the earnings of Bell amounting to many millions of dollars each year, is a fair arrangement for the people of Canada and the users of the Bell Telephone services.
All of these matters which concern the national interest ought to be gone into by the committee with the greatest possible care. We should be satisfied that Bell is prepared to undertake to make its operations consonant with the national interest before this tremendous extension of power and financial base is given to the company by this parliament.
As a result of its incorporation almost 90 years ago the Bell Telephone Company is able to use and enjoy a natural monopoly, as I have said, over the major part of this country. Even now, if I may say so, in my view as a lawyer it has exceeded the powers given it in 1880 and in every amendment I have seen to its initial act of incorporation. It has carried on activities which are beyond the powers it has had until now. In my opinion it has not had the power under its act of incorporation and the amendments to that act to go into the field of telecommunications, a field it has entered without the authority that it ought to have sought from this parliament.
To a large extent, Mr. Speaker, this bill is now asking parliament to rubberstamp and to give the company authority to carry on activities which it has to date carried on without such authority. This is one of the reasons that it no longer wants to go to the Board of Transport Commissioners over the question of issuing shares. It wants to have more and more freedom. This parliament, and I suggest the people of Canada as well, must be assured that that freedom will be used to the benefit of this country, not merely to increase the net income and earnings of this company.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I was struck by words used in one of the clauses of this bill. I am not going to refer to the actual provision as such but merely to the phrase which caught my attention. In clause 7 of the

February 16, 1967
Private Bills
bill certain things are proposed, namely, the extension of the activities of this company in the entire field of telecommunications. At the end of the clause it is stated that things may be done which in the opinion of the board of directors are "deemed to be in the interest of the company".
I am not concerned, Mr. Speaker, about the interest of this company. I want to make sure, and this parliament ought to make sure, that the extension of this company's activities into the various aspects of telecommunications is in the interest of Canada, not merely in the interest of Bell. Under this bill the board of directors is empowered to take steps to make extensions which they deem to be in the interest of Bell. The things Bell has done up to now have been in its own interest and frequently against the interest of the Canadian people, and it is time the situation was reversed.
This company seeks power to extend its monopoly into various fields. I submit we cannot approve this kind of extension of monopolistic power on the part of such a giant without certain safeguards, Mr. Speaker, and I will mention only a few.
It is our firm belief and conviction that a company like Bell, performing the kind of service it performs, ought to have on its board of directors public representatives appointed by parliament or the government. They should be members of the board who represent the public and are prohibited from having any financial interest in the company or in any of its subsidiaries. This will ensure that on the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company there are men and women who represent the people of Canada and who have no personal interest in the financial and earnings arrangements of the company or its subsidiaries.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
We ought to have a guarantee in this act that Bell will not enter the field of broadcasting, even though it may have facilities that may be used for broadcasting. We now have the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, private television, radio stations and networks; we do not want a giant like Bell to enter that field as well and start new difficulties and new conflicts in this country. We should have provision in the act incorporating this company for Bell to disclose in detail the operations and earnings of all its subsidiaries. Let us have no more of these unrevealing, consolidated statements that hide everything which should be known by parliament and

the people of Canada. We ought to have a provision to give us all the information about Northern Electric and all the other companies that Bell now owns, or is likely to acquire under the proposed clause 8 of the bill. We should have a guarantee from Bell respecting the added capitalization it seeks, that any research work it will do will be research work done in Canada, that the powers we give the company may be used for the development of technological research and knowhow for the service of the Canadian people.
We ought to be sure that it will not use that money to buy the results of research elsewhere by making another service contract with American Telephone & Telegraph, or some other company in the United States, Britain, or elsewhere in the world. When it boasts about its intention to do research work, we ought to be certain that that research work will be done in this country, and that the results of the work are available to this country. We ought to have many other, similar safeguards before this already too big giant is made bigger still.

speechtext:
I do not argue with his appraisal of the problem. He was fair. He did not make unsubstantiated charges but posed many pertinent questions to which he felt the
House of Commons and the Canadian people should know the answers. Nobody in the house who is the least bit objective can argue that Canada and Canadians, through the medium of parliament, should not be fully protected, and should not have the right to know the answers to many of the questions asked by the hon. member for York South.
When the matter comes before the committee I think the hon. member will be pleased to know that, in all probability, many of the questions he has asked today are already on public record. The answers to many other questions will do much to allay his fears about giant corporations.
My philosophy about corporations is different from that of the hon. member; but, we respect each other's views on this matter. I am particularly concerned about and interested in the relationship between Northern Electric and other subsidiaries. I was surprised to learn from the hon. member's speech-and I know this must be accurate or he would not have said it-that Bell has financial interests in 15 or 16 subsidiaries.

subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: Sixteen.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
I hope that Bell treats all its subsidiaries with the same consideration and respect it shows to Northern Electric and its employees. If Bell's relationship with its many subsidiaries is as fruitful, objective and fair as its relationship with Northern Electric, or at least with the employees of Northern Electric, I shall be pleased. If this information is brought out in committee, then the suggestion of the hon. member to refer this to a committee will have been valuable.
It might be good to know that the request in the bill that Bell be permitted to lend money to its employees and to help in the field of housing is not a new departure for that company. It has had similar relations with its employees, and the committee might be glad to know that.
Private Bills
I do not intend to answer the hon. member's questions because I do not know the answers. I know that the questions were asked in a spirit of objectivity. I know that the development of Northern Electric came about through a need. Companies such as Bell Telephone, which operate as a monopoly but which are regulated by government boards, such as the Department of Transport and other boards, do not justify their existence for any reason except that they are in business to make money. In a free enterprise system this is a logical reason for any company, big or small, to be in business. Bell's rate of profit is regulated to protect the Canadian people, because the company has a monopolistic position. Northern Electric was created essentially to fulfil a need, to make available to the Bell Telephone Company from sources within Canada parts, pieces, components and knowhow that could not be obtained here when Northern Electric was formed. This may not be the situation today. It is conceivable, had Bell Telephone been formed today, that with our increased population, more developed economy and increased technological knowledge it would not have been necessary to form this close alliance with a company such as Northern Electric.
The hon. member mentioned research. When this matter is aired in committee I know that we shall be pleased to find that as the result of research in Canada and inventions coming from that research, the Bell Telephone Company and Northern Electric account for a very substantial export business, when measured in dollars and cents.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
As the hon. member for York South mentioned, the shares of Bell Telephone are widely dispersed. It is good to think we have a corporation in Canada 94 per cent of whose shares are owned by Canadians and in the hands of 240,000 Canadians, among an investing population probably no greater than half a million. To me, this indicates the high regard felt by the people of Canada for Bell Telephone. Of course most members of parliament, including myself, gripe occasionally at the service they receive, and get letters from constituents occasionally raising particular problems; but in general I believe the relationship between this country and the Bell Telephone Company is a good one.
As was pointed out during the course of a similar discussion last year, if the Bell

February 16, 1967
Private Bills
Telephone Company were ever to be nationalized

and I do not think anyone in the house would suggest such a thing-it is highly doubtful whether the Canadian people would be half as well served as they are today under this private enterprise system of ours. I invite hon. members to compare the record of the company from this point of view-remembering that it shows a profit ratio of 6.6 per cent-with that of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or any other Crown corporation.
I am as anxious as is the hon. member for York South to see this matter referred to the appropriate committee so that these questions can be cleared up once and for all. If I am a member of that committee-and I want to make this clear-I will take a dim view of any action which would in any way adversely affect Northern Electric and the employees of that company. I say this regardless of whether its relationship to the Bell Telephone Company is improper in the eyes of some people. I must admit my bias. Living close to Northern Electric I am fully aware of the contribution the company has made to the social and economic development of my city and of the area directly concerned. The relationship of the company with its employees has been laudable and one which other corporations might well seek to emulate. Participation by the company in the social activities of the community has been most beneficial. Its willingness to take part in the activities of the 19 communities on Montreal Island, and I am sure, in other regions, has always been evident; the company has acted unselfishly and with the minimum of publicity for the good of the community. As far as I am concerned, Northern Electric have been good corporate citizens.
I would urge the house to take advantage of the remaining few moments by recommending that the bill be sent to the appropriate committee, so that we can seek out answers to many of the questions which were so objectively and eloquently asked by the hon. member for York South.

speechtext:
When I look at the bill before us I find myself concerned by the reference in some of its clauses to telecommunications. Some hon. members have already drawn attention to the implications of the changes proposed. It appears to me that on the basis of these provisions the company can now go into broadcasting. This is an aspect which should be examined by the committee on broadcasting.

The bill speaks of the power to transmit, which includes the emission or reception of signs, signals, writing, images, sounds, and so on, whether visual or auditory. This does seem perilously close to transmissions of the sort we have already heard about in the broadcasting committee-community antenna television and educational television, for example. Since, in the near future educational television and community antenna television may be brought under the Broadcasting Act, I am inclined to support those hon. members who advocate a close look at clauses 7 and 8 to see exactly what their implications are.
When dealing with this field of telecommunications we must not forget that a network of telecommunications belonging to the Canadian National already exists in this country. I will leave the implications of monopoly to be discussed by others; some hon. members have already spoken very well on this subject. Generally, I would support the observations the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) has made in connection with Northern Electric, but I would point out that if the bill before us allows a virtual monopoly in the field of coaxial cables, other firms who produce coaxial cables in this country, such as Industrial Wire and Cable, will find great difficulty in breaking into the market now that a wholly owned subsidiary is able to supply all the needs of this large corporation.
In closing, I return to this question of transmission lines. I would remind hon. members that in Britain transmission lines and microwave systems used by the B.B.C. are publicly owned; it is only those operated by private stations which are owned by I.T.V. the private organization. We should look closely at anything which might place one company in control of educational television, or even for that matter of community antenna television systems.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that I do not see the parliamentary, secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) here at the moment, because I should like to make a comment or two about his speech and I should like to do so in his presence. Not having any control over the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour, however, I expect I will have to go ahead in his absence. I listened with a great deal of interest to what he had to say about the bill. I should like to commend him, inasmuch as he was speaking from a position of semi-government, for his endorsation of the views expressed by the hon. member for
February 16, 1967

York South (Mr. Lewis). It is gratifying to have a man who is half way into the cabinet endorse the concept of public representatives on the board of directors of this particular company. We look forward to having the support of the parliamentary secretary and others of his party for these proposals when the bill is considered in the committee.
I think the parliamentary secretary's tangent-like comment with regard to state ownership, when he compared public ownership of a corporation such as the Bell Telephone Company with the ownership of the C.B.C., is an impossible equation. I am sure he knew it and just tossed it out in order to fill in some space. I do not believe he was really sincere in suggesting that it would be possible to make any such comparison, and thus try to play down the great benefits which can come from ownership of certain utilities.
I was also quite struck by his love affair with the Northern Electric Company. As he said, he is a bit prejudiced and biased in this regard. I should think that would be sufficient to disclose his real interest in the Northern Electric Company. I think, as he said, that he threw this in because of his own prejudice and I do not believe it in any way detracts from the substance of his remarks at the outset when he endorsed the views of the hon. member for York South, which views were exceptionally well expressed.
After listening to the hon. member for York South, I feel somewhat the way I feel after my wife has finished speaking to me-there is not much left to say. There is a matter here, however, which I think should concern us, and that is the size of the company and the implications it has in respect of our economy, especially the economy in sections of our country in which the Bell Telephone Company operates. We must remember that this company does not operate directly in the four western provinces. At home, in my own province, we have a privately owned corporation, the B.C. Telephone Company. In the other provinces there are publicly owned telephone systems. When one considers that the operations of the Bell Telephone Company are confined to only a section of our economy and a geographical section of Canada, their request for an increase in capitalization to $lf billion is made even more important. This is especially true when we realize that $1| billion, being the requested capitalization of Bell Telephone Company, represents just about one quarter of the total budget of the government and the parliament
Private Bills
of Canada. When we think in terms of that capitalization being a quarter of the total budget of Canada, and when we remember that Bell Telephone carries on its activities in only a portion of Canada, this carries with it that much more significance and that much more impact and should, I think, lead us more definitely to an understanding that what really exists here, and what has developed since 1880 when I believe the company was first incorporated by a private act, is not only a monopoly but a structure within which private and not public law is involved.
I believe we are giving, and over the years have given, to Bell Telephone Company authority which equals in all respects the authority of the government. This has been done by giving to this company practically the right to initiate its own system of law making, in so far as the bounds of the statutes relating to the Bell Telephone Company permit this. That, coupled with the size of this company and the revolution which has taken place in the telecommunications, electronics, television and other fields, should convince us that a company of this magnitude and with this much power and authority in its grasp ought to have on its board of directors representatives who would protect the interests of the public. This theory and idea was advanced by my friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) and others in this party during an earlier parliament and gained a great deal of support in the house.
For reasons which I do not have to go into at this moment, because it is nearly seven o'clock and I do not wish to impede the progress of the bill at this stage, it was felt at that time that it was desirable to withdraw the proposal for including public representatives on the board of directors of Bell Telephone Company. This attitude was adopted partly because there was very little warning. Inasmuch as that warning was given in an earlier parliament I am sure the Bell Telephone Company will not be surprised when they are asked at the time the bill reaches the committee to endorse this proposal, that the government appoint public representatives to the board of directors.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on transport and communications.

Mr. Chairman, before the hour for private bills intervened I was bringing to the minister's attention the fact that he had not exploited the opportunities offered by the increasing productivity in Canada, to the extent that we on this side of the house feel he should have.
Had such emphasis been placed we would not have received the lecture which was given to us tonight, in which the minister indicated the sums of money that would be

DEBATES	February 16, 1967
required for the kinds of programs which everyone in this country agrees are necessary for the nation. I should like to indicate to the minister that since our productivity is about 25 per cent lower than that of the United States-and there is very little reason for this-an increase in that productivity to bring it up to a level comparable to that in the United States, not only at the federal level but at all levels, would bring in an increase of about $4 billion in taxes, using approximately the same rates, because an increase in our gross national product without changing the level of rates in this country would certainly give us a tremendous increase in tax revenues at all levels-municipal, provincial and federal.
It seems to me that the inflation which we are experiencing in Canada would have provided an excellent opportunity for the minister to have introduced measures for increasing our productivity, measures which under circumstances of unemployment are very difficult to implement but under situations of excess demand could have been carried out. However, he did not take that opportunity to bring in those measures and I think he should be taken to task somewhat for that omission. Canada, however, is a different country-and this is something that our governments have not recognized in the past-with distinct problems requiring answers suitable to its own circumstances.
If the U.S. economy could afford 10 firms of a particular size necessary for mass production, it should be obvious that anything more than one of these in Canada would not achieve the possible efficiencies. Even when we acknowledge the need for such giants, our reluctance to supervise monopoly led us to encourage pygmies. The kind of competition that developed behind our tariff walls was a strange fish: It spawned factories which produced almost every range and variety of product that was being produced in the U.S., but in miniature replica. Every major U.S. manufacturer, especially in consumer goods, rushed to put his brand in the Canadian market, ensuring his share of the second most affluent consumers in the world.
To reinforce this pattern came advertising. It ensured that Canadian consumers would be told that they must live exactly like the Americans, accepting all the products and values of American ingenuity. We are on a permanent treadmill, U.S. ownership or not, unless we can change this topsy-like pattern to one of a planned structure.

subtopic: BROADENING OF LENDING PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the measure before the house is to add a further three year period during which loans made by chartered banks under this act may be guaranteed by the government and to extend the scope of the act in order to make its benefits available to a large number of small businesses.
I am sure hon. members will recall that this act was passed in 1961 to empower the government to guarantee loans made by chartered banks to small businesses engaged in manufacturing, trade or services for purchasing equipment and improving or enlarging the premises in which they operate. An amendment in 1962 extended the purposes for which loans may be made to include the purchase or building of premises, where existing premises cease to be available, or where a new site is necessary for the normal development of the business.
Under the terms of the act, a small business enterprise is that with an estimated annual gross revenue not exceeding $250,000. The maximum amount that can be borrowed at any time is $25,000 and loans are payable over a period of at most ten years. The maximum interest rate that can be charged on those loans is set by the regulations. It has been at 5J per cent since the beginning of this program.
The act became effective on January 19, 1961 for an initial period of about three years ending on December 31, 1964. It authorized the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) to guarantee any bank against loss of an amount not exceeding 10 per cent of all the business improvement loans granted by the bank over the lending period. Provision was made for a total of $300 million for all loans that chartered banks could grant under the act during the lending period. The act was amended in 1963 so as to provide an additional three year lending period during which guaranteed loans could be made under the

DEBATES	February 16. 1967
same conditions as during the original lending period. The legislation now before the house will provide for another lending period which will extend from January 1, 1967 to January 31, 1969. During this further period, the same guarantee provisions will continue to apply just as during each of the two previous guarantee periods.
Due to the pressure of current business in the house, it was not possible to introduce the resolution preceding this bill before the middle of December 1966 and the schedule of legislation precluded discussion before the Christmas and New Year adjournment. In order to prevent stoppage of the operations being conducted under this legislation, the bill carries a clause making the application of this legislation retroactive to January 1, 1967. Meanwhile, the Minister of Finance has asked the chartered banks to continue lending under the act, pending the passage of the present bill and the minister has been assured by the banks that they would.
The other provisions of the bill concern the scope of lending operations under the Small Businesses Loans Act. They deal with points which may have contributed to the little use made of that act until now.
Every year from the implementation of the act until 1965, chartered banks have granted some 3,000 loans to small businesses, totalling $26 million. Although the final figures for 1966 are not yet available, it seems at first glance that loans in 1966 totalled $21 million. Therefore, during the six first years the act has been in operation an approximate total of $150 million has been granted in loans. Of course, it is not an unimportant amount and it has probably been quite beneficial to borrowers. But it might be possible that it is not a valid sign of the entire potential demand which could exist for such loans.
The rather moderate application of this act is mostly due to a few characteristics of its provisions and the purpose of this legislation is to amend those main features, in order to extend the application of the act to a greater number of small businesses.
A rather secondary factor, which explains the relatively limited use of this act, is the fact that the purposes for which loans could normally be granted included improvement or extension of premises. As I said earlier, the act admitted only the purchase or the building of replacement premises, when the premises used up to then were no longer available. Unusual situations arose from that. For example, the owner of a retail store
February 16, 1967	COMMONS
operating in rented space was not able, under the act, to finance the purchase of the building in which he had settled down, although he could, under the same act, finance the purchase of a building across the street if he was to evacuate the premises he was occupying. The new bill aims at extending the present grounds for loans, in order to allow the purchase and the construction of premises in every case and not only under the circumstances I just mentioned.
Another more significant factor is that the loans at present can only be granted to the small businesses engaged in manufacturing, wholesale, retail, and service. There are several other small businesses engaged in construction, transportation and communications that are not at present eligible for loans, under the act, but the nature of which would permit them to avail themselves of such loans, as well as the retailer or the small manufacturer. The bill provides eligibility to guaranted loans for the small business enterprises falling into these three classes.
A third factor is the present limitation on the size of the small business for eligibility. Such enterprise was defined as having an annual gross revenue not exceeding $250,000. Sometimes, particularly in the case of some retailers and wholesalers, this led to an arbitrary exclusion of businesses which, in other respects, could have qualified for loans under this act. The legislation before us changes the definition of the small business eligible in determining that its estimated annual gross revenue shall not exceed $500,000.
However, I wish to point to hon. members that there is at present no provision for increasing the maximum amount of a loan permissible under the act. In deciding to leave the amount unchanged, the government has taken into consideration other financing sources available to companies needing more than $25,000, one of these being, of course, the Industrial Development Bank. The Small Businesses Loans Act is designed particularly for very small business concerns, where the owner ordinarily deals with the local bank branch for all his financial needs. All the more reason why we must expect businesses needing over $25,000 and those having a turnover exceeding $500,000 to have plans that require financing beyond the scope of the Small Businesses Loans Act. Such projects can be financed either by individual lenders or by the Industrial Development Bank. Of course, borrowers at the intermediate level will prefer loans governed by the Small
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment Businesses Loans Act, since banks cannot charge more than 5J per cent on loans granted under this act, as compared to higher rates charged by individual lenders and the Industrial Development Bank.
This brings me to another point which, I think, is important. The purpose of the government guarantee, as authorized by the act, is to encourage the banks to earmark, for a given period, a portion of their funds for loans intended for business improvement. However, that provision gives less and less incentive, at a time when the level of interest has substantially increased, while the interest rate on guaranteed loans to small businesses remains at 5J, per cent.
That rate, of course, was set initially on the basis of the 6 per cent ceiling of the interest rate provided by the Bank Act, at a time when the interest rates were generally substantially below the present level. It is unquestionable that the bank rate, under the act, must take into account the guarantee granted to those loans by the government. However, if the act must still benefit truly the small borrowing businesses, the rate must be sensibly determined in proportion to the rates charged by the banks without government guarantee, after the ceiling on interest charges has been modified by the bank legislation which is before the house. Once that measure has been passed and new interest rates have been set, the minister proposes to review the interest rate provided by the act and to recommend to the governor in council, if necessary, a change in the administration rule in order to set a new maximum rate under the Small Businesses Loans Act.
I believe that the average businessmen will welcome this initiative even if it involves a higher interest rate. At the present time, several business men find that they cannot get all, or part of the funds they need, at an interest rate of 5| per cent and they have no other alternative than to turn toward other means of financing which are considerably more costly. Such an initiative will evidently reduce the difference between the rates imposed on loans granted under the Small Businesses Loans Act and those demanded by the private lenders or by the Industrial Development Bank. The cost of a loan granted under the Small Businesses Loans Act will become a little less advantageous, but the funds available under that act will be increased.
Mr. Chairman, this brings me to the conclusion of the remarks I wanted to make at this stage.

These agricultural societies have provincial charters and if they do not receive aid under this legislation they will disappear. I hope in the near future, by means of this or other legislation, we will be able to assist them.
I am informed that the former minister of agriculture had intended to introduce a program to set up loan facilities for these societies. This has not been done. Perhaps it could be done by means of this legislation. I will have more to say later concerning this new legislation, but this will conclude my remarks at this time.
