speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in opening my remarks I would first of all like to congratulate the parliamentary secretary upon his lucid explanation of this legislation. It has been most helpful. I also wish to indicate the
13144	COMMONS
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment general approval of this resolution by the members of this party. We believe it is a most worth-while piece of legislation. It has proven Its value in the past and I am sure it will assume increasing importance in the future. It is particularly important that the government has recognized the changing role of the small businessman by moving the ceiling from $250,000 to $500,000 because, although we speak of the small businessman and think of his business in terms of infinitesimal sales, the truth is that in many cases today the amount of capital required by even the smaller businesses in our society has expanded enormously, and this resolution takes this into account.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I am also pleased to note that the restrictions in respect of the use of this money have been removed, so far as the construction and communication industries are concerned. The government should have gone further and included other industries, and I intend to discuss this aspect a little later this evening. Small businesses today form an important part of our society and I am sure they will continue to play an important role in our industrial and commercial system.
Statistics indicate that small businesses today make up more than 94 to 100 per cent of the number of industries in most fields of business activity. Although we have witnessed tremendous growth of giant corporations, prospects and needs for small businesses apparently have not diminished. If we consider small businesses with assets of less than $1 million, we find there are some 440,000 small businesses in Canada, most of them unincorporated, with assets under $100,000. A great many of them are engaged in the retail trade, service or construction industries.
I said earlier that it was important to remove the restriction in the application of this measure in respect of the construction industry. There are many efficient contractors in business who will benefit from this measure, and will be able to play an important role in alleviating the serious shortage of houses that exists in this country.
There is a particular need today for special legislation to help small businesses. As the government learns to use and apply monetary and fiscal tools to manage the economy the tendency will exist to tighten the screws on small businesses more so than on larger corporate organizations. The government should go further than it has in terms of laying down guide lines to the banks, which are charged

DEBATES	February 16, 1967
with the responsibility of carrying out the provisions of this legislation so that under the special circumstances of monetary or fiscal tightness the small businessman does not bear the greatest load.
Anyone who has observed what has happened in the markets when money is tightened to control difficulties of an economic nature must recognize that the small businessman is worse off than others. For that reason special consideration must be given. Small businessmen frequently lack alternate sources of credit. The royal commission which studied this problem pointed that out. Larger corporations can float bonds and go to special organizations for money. They can also increase their stock offerings and take advantage of many other sources of money. In many cases they can use their retained earnings. These sources of money are not always available to small businesses, therefore the function of the bank is of paramount importance.
The government has indicated to the chartered banks of Canada its desire to help small businesses. They must be aware of the government's concern in this regard. Following the changes to the Bank Act the situation will become more difficult for the small operator. His bargaining position will not be as great vis-a-vis banks.
In the long run this kind of legislation will be very helpful to the government in obtaining support for its broader proposals under the Bank Act. One thing which has disturbed many of us about the changes to that act is the problem of how small businesses are going to exert sufficient influence under the flexible arrangement proposed by the government to ensure that they have adequate access to funds at reasonable rates. We all realize that money is available at extremely high rates. Small businesses cannot afford to pay these high costs. This act will help to satisfy those of us who have been concerned about difficulties which may be created by the provisions of the new banking legislation.
Let me make two suggestions at this time. I have indicated my general support for the measure before us. There are, however, omissions of an important nature in terms of the future of small businesses. Funds should be made available to small companies for the purchase of other like companies in order that they may enlarge their operations. There is nothing in this bill which would permit such activities. Anyone who is familiar with the operations of small businesses knows that
February 16, 1967
they represent the largest untapped reservoir of managerial talent that exists in this country. Anyone who has tried to operate a small business will appreciate that it is more difficult to operate a small business than a large one.
With advances in technology there is an increased need to enlarge operations. What might have been efficient at one time becomes less efficient with changing technological requirements. Small businesses require more capital and a great deal more management. I think we should allow the small companies in our business community to take advantage of opportunities, and provide funds in order that they may expand. The omission of such a provision in this measure is something that should be corrected. Surely this would be valuable to our economic future. This would allow able and talented managers to develop their operations and provide increased efficiency in some areas. It would certainly enable them to act with a greater degree of knowledge and technology.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The other suggestion I should like to make is this. Since this program provides a great deal of assistance to small businessmen, two things should be done. First it should be given increased publicity. I do not think enough business operators in this country are aware of the provisions of this act and the fact that the parliament of Canada has already passed legislation of this type and will probably pass similar legislation in future. I believe they should be made aware of this fact. This may be one of the reasons that the amounts authorized by the legislation have never been fully taken up.
The other suggestion I should like to make in this regard is that these loans carry an insurance charge. At the present time a loss is sustained from the operation of this fund. This loss is met out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund. I refer to the loss sustained in the lending of money under the conditions prescribed in the act. Last year, if I am correct, the amount of loss was $76,785. This is not a large amount; it is not an amount that perhaps should arouse an excessive degree of concern. But I believe there is a principle involved here. Those of us in parliament are looking at this legislation from the viewpoint of providing every possible assistance to the small businessman, and there should not be any subsidy feature in the program as far as the government or the taxpayers of this country are concerned.
23033-831J
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment
Although the loss experienced is rather small and is, I would think, a very good indication of the healthy state of our business community generally, and the considered use of this fund by our banks, I believe that loans made under the act should be insured. The premium charged should be sufficient to cover this kind of loss, so as to make the entire program self-sustaining. We adopt this principle in connection with other government programs. We do it with home improvements and N.H.A. loans, and I believe it would be a logical extension of that principle to apply it also to this legislation.
Looking at the loss experience, according to the report of 1965, of 14,050 loans made, 25 were in default. If you figure out the actual amount of default, it works out to one tenth of one per cent, as close as I can get it. I quote these figures as an indication of the small amount of the loss and the small premium that would be necessary to ensure that the loans are fully covered and represent no charge on general revenues. This program would then be completely self-sufficient. I believe most businessmen would view this proposal with favour. They would consider that a small charge of this type to insure loans would be acceptable. And it would go a long way toward improving the conception of this kind of program.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like again to voice our support of this most valuable piece of legislation. I would urge the government to consider the suggestions we have made for the purpose of improving the provisions of this act, and hope the government will bring in recommendations in the future to implement these suggestions.

Mr. Chairman, as usual, I will not take too much time at the resolution stage precisely because we do not yet have the bill. This time, however, the terms of the proposed legislation are clear enough to indicate what will be provided for in the bill, and I should like to congratulate the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in particular for his work.
Naturally, this legislation is simply a broadening of the act passed in 1961 under the Conservative government; it was amended in 1963 and this year it will be extended to December 31, 1969. Mr. Chairman, I believe the parliamentary secretary will certainly be happy, since the bill will receive unanimous: approval, and it is always pleasant when one

13146	COMMONS
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment makes a proposal with the assurance that *discussions will not be too lengthy. That is understandable, when we are presented with legislation favouring our interests, the interests of Canadian citizens; it is not at all like being asked to pass a measure causing hardship. We prefer to support this proposal rather than pass a bill resulting in increased taxes, because an increase in taxes is always hard on the people. I therefore wish to congratulate the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance.
This gesture on the part of the government will surely help small businesses, which daily need more help because, on the whole, the government is not assuming an extraordinary responsibility, since its liability is only 10 per cent. In my opinion, this is not excessive. [DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Even if the government had wanted, while introducing its amendment, to give greater satisfaction to the small businessmen in increasing a little the government's endorsing responsibilities, it would not have taken a great risk as far as money is concerned, because a businessman who makes a loan of $25,000, while he is worth $200,000, $250,000 or $300,000, is not a great financial risk.
I feel that the difficulty will lie in fixing the bank interest rate. It is understood that if the present rate provided by the law, that is 5J per cent, is maintained, I do not think a single bank would be interested in making loans. In fact, I have discussed the matter several times with some of my electors. They had visited me to obtain a loan, and I can assure you, sir, that at the rate of 5J per cent, the banks became more and more disinterested, for it should not be forgotten that today the bank lends at rates of 8 and 8J per cent. People say that the interest rate is 7 per cent, but there are also the administrative costs. The banks are entitled to charge for administration, and they will do it quite willingly.
To my knowledge, most small manufacturers-perhaps 80 per cent of them-having obtained loans applied directly to the banks, since the banks could not make up their minds and accept the government's requirements. Even though the government was the endorser, the banks would rather run the risk, which, in my opinion, was rather non-existent. They preferred running the risk, if any, and lend at 8 and 84 per cent.
That is why I am reminding the minister he must consider which interest rate will be more acceptable to the banks, because it is useless to pass a piece of legislation while

DEBATES	February 16, 1967
knowing beforehand that it will be impossible to implement it through lack of interest on the part of the banks.
Anyone in their place would not reason otherwise, because the real purpose of banks is to administer their business; their purpose is to make money rather than to suffer losses, even though the government itself advises them to that effect.
If I were a bank manager and the government advised me to lend money at 5| per cent, I can assure you that if I had the chance to charge an 8 per cent interest, I would certainly do so.
Since nothing is decided yet, in this bill, I suggest that the minister be very careful so as to avoid making this legislation ineffective. These loans are surely more advantageous than those of the Industrial Development Bank, because I think that an enterprise must be in a very difficult position to borrow from the Industrial Development Bank under the conditions offered these days.
Nowadays, if you borrow from the Industrial Development Bank, they will first try to retain a reserve of $2,500 which will be remitted after ten years, if you will, but such $2,500 will be kept in reserve and interest charged on the balance. The borrower will get only $23,500 and the $2,500 will be loaned for ten years.
Now, our bill must prevent tricks of that kind. Banks should not be forced to accept profits on the side. If our legislation is very clear, well defined and if the interests are very obvious and do not cause banks to lose money, I believe the tricks like the ones we see in the Industrial Development Bank will not be repeated. I have known some of the things certain industrialists were asking for. They finally obtained the amounts they were looking for. Now, when an industrialist needs $25,000 more and sees $2,500 of that amount held back, that is not satisfactory at all.
Mr. Chairman, I would also like to draw the attention of the government on the small businesses in our areas. This is a good piece of legislation, but I think that something more should be done in order to save private enterprise in the province of Quebec; I do not know how it fares in the other provinces, but as far as Quebec is concerned, there are serious problems with respect to private enterprise, tremendous difficulties when it comes to securing capital at a reasonable rate. I hope that the government will not merely extend the effects of the legislation already passed, but that it will try to find new ways
February 16, 1967	COMMONS
of expanding our private enterprises a little more.

subtopic: BROADENING OF LENDING PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 would like to say a few words on this resolution, which makes provision for amendment to the Small Businesses Loans Act. For many years the small businessman, who has been a very important part of our economy, has been forgotten. There was no legislation on the order paper and no legislation was passed through the house to make loans available to him. And yet, Mr. Chairman, the small businessman, as has been said so many times during this debate, is an important part of our national economy. He is the one who goes to the newly developed areas and brings the goods and services that are so necessary to the development of these areas. He is the man who takes the lead in the municipalities, does work in his church, his schoolboard and commissions. He is the man who throughout the years, as great corporations, chain stores and big manufacturers grew and developed in this country, found it more and more difficult to be competitive. There was no government assistance available to him. Farmers had their farm credit corporations, big manufacturers, and the industrialists had the Industrial Development Bank, but the small businessman had nowhere to go for loans except to his local bank.
Those of us who are small businessmen and who have tried to get loans from chartered banks without having too much collateral have found it pretty difficult. However, the government of which I was a supporter and which came into power in 1958 realized that this was an area which needed assistance. So, in 1958, a branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce, called the small businesses branch, was set up. This was the branch where the problems of small business were discussed, and to which small businessmen could send in their requests and have them answered. I might say that this function is being performed in the Province of Ontario by the department of planning and development. This department has provided assistance to communities all across Ontario by analysing the businesses of small businessmen and providing helpful suggestions in their operations. This has been very valuable assistance in the last two or three years in the Province of Ontario.
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment
As I said, the Conservative party realized in 1958 the importance of the small businessman in our national economy and did something about it. In fact, four days after the opening of parliament in November of 1966 the Speech from the Throne was postponed so as to bring in Bill C-40 which initiated the Small Businesses Loans Act, This was a very important piece of legislation particularly in view of the high rise of unemployment in 1957 and 1958 which we inherited from the previous government. In this connection I should like to read the statement made by Hon. Donald Fleming when Bill C-40 was first introduced in the house. It indicates that the Conservative party of that day was ready and willing to do all that it could to overcome some of the problems with which it was faced. He said the following:
My ministers are convinced that additional medium-term credit facilities for small businesses would enable many private projects to go forward this winter all across Canada, providing substantial additional employment. Moreover, this addition to our credit legislation will constitute a continuing stimulus to the growth of Canadian private enterprises.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Now, Mr. Chairman, this is a very important piece of legislation which provides assistance to a group of people who never had any provision made for them before by way of government loans. This act made it possible for them to go to chartered banks and get assistance it they wanted to remodel their store facilities or, if they were in a service industry, to buy a new piece of equipment. These business people would thereby be enabled to meet the competition of larger, more powerful chain stores or bigger service industries.
However, Mr. Chairman, as is the case with a lot of new legislation there had to be a trial period and, as the parliamentary secretary indicated, this bill had to be amended in 1962 to make it possible for people who were in small businesses to move to new premises. This Small Businesses Loans Act has not been as useful or as comprehensive an act as it should be. This fact is indicated by an article in the Ottawa Citizen of June 25 which is headed, "Small Loans to Business off $359,048". This same situation is reflected in an article in Men's Wear magazine which indicates that in the first nine months of this year, small business operators borrowed only $15.1 million compared with $19.8 million in the same period of 1965.
13148	COMMONS
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment
There are several reasons for this situation.
I believe one was indicated here tonight, namely the fact that the interest rate is only 5.5 per cent. Probably the banks were not as happy lending money at 5.5 per cent when they could get more for it from other areas. There has been some feeling amongst people who applied for these loans that the regulations were a little too stringent. In addition, as someone said tonight, there was a feeling not enough publicity had been given to this act and there were not enough small businessmen in Canada who knew about this particular piece of legislation.
However, Mr. Chairman, we are very happy tonight to learn there is going to be an extension of this act to make it possible for people engaged in the construction, transportation and communication businesses to participate in these loans. These people will be allowed now to purchase or construct new premises. I believe the lack of this provision has been a detriment to this piece of legislation. I remember many cases in which people wanted to start up in business but were not able to get a loan of this type, because they had not been in business before. I feel that the extension of this act is going to be of great help to many small businessmen in Canada by increasing the number of people who can participate.
However, Mr. Chairman, I believe there is still room for improvement in this legislation. One of these is the need for working capital for some types of service industries. For instance, a man who goes into furniture manufacturing in a small way may use most of his own capital to buy his equipment and purchase his first order or raw material. He has to give credit to his furniture dealers for 60 or 90 days, and during that period he may have to pay for his raw material and equipment, as well as meet his payroll. He often finds himself pinched for funds. Here is a business which, if a few thousand dollars of working capital were provided during this period, may prove successful. I believe the local banker would not have any compunction about helping an industry of that type because in a good many of these small communities the banker has an intimate knowledge of the operator.
I have knowledge of an example of this type of thing. There was a chap who started a furniture business and who knew what he was doing. He came to this particular period in the initial development of the operation when he was pinched for capital. The bank, because of regulations, could not give him

DEBATES	February 16, 1967
any working capital and he was going to have to go to the money markets and probably pay 10 per cent or 15 per cent interest. If working capital were made available during this initial period, it would mean the difference between success and failure for this business.
There is one other area in which I should like to suggest there is room for improvement. When this act was first introduced the maximum amount of loans was $25,000. This might have been realistic in 1960 when the scope of the act was limited to small manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers or service industries. Now, however, the act is being extended to construction, transportation and communications industries. I have not had too much experience with this type of business, but a $25,000 loan to a man in the construction business who wants to buy a bulldozer, for instance, is not of much use. How far will a loan of that amount go for a man in the transportation business who wants to buy a diesel truck? Of how much assistance is it?
I feel there is room for improvement in these two particular areas. I hope the parliamentary secretary will bring these two cases to the attention of the minister and that the minister will give them consideration. Then, this bill will not be too stringent but will make it possible for small businessmen to participate in these loans. This legislation should look after a group of people who have been forgotten for many years. We will support the resolution as it is. As I say, it is our job as an opposition to indicate the areas in which legislation that is being introduced could be improved. I do feel, Mr. Chairman, that with the addition of these two areas I have suggested, this particular resolution which has to do with the amendment of the Small Businesses Loans Act will be more effective.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two brief observations. First I should like to congratulate the parliamentary secretary upon his statement introducing the resolution this evening, and also my colleague who has just spoken, the hon. member for Welhngton-Huron who drew to the attention of the house the steps the Conservative government took in 1961 to introduce this most worth-while piece of legislation. I think each of us in this house who comes from a community in which there are many small businessmen has seen the usefulness of this act demonstrated. I think of family businesses that have been handed down from father to
February 16, 1967
son, and this act has enabled them to carry on. I think of some of the new Canadians who came to Canada without capital but brought with them their skills and trades and who, as a result of loans obtained under this act, have been able to start up small businesses or manufacturing concerns. Corner grocery stores and confectionery stores, and so on, have derived great advantage under this act. I can recall main streets in small communities whose appearance has been greatly improved by the erection of new store fronts financed by loans under this act. Therefore I congratulate the government upon broadening its terms to include assistance in construction, transportation and communications. A small business operator can borrow under this act now to purchase or construct a building.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
All in all, Mr. Chairman, this has been a good piece of legislation. But it should be better; it still does not have the potential it should have. I am not sure where the trouble lies. Maybe, part of the problem has been that the act is applicable only to those businesses with up to $250,000 gross sales per year. The government is now stepping this figure up to $500,000 and more businesses will become eligible for the benefits of the act.
However, Mr. Chairman, this is still not enough. The government must sell this legislation and must ask the bank managers why more people are not taking advantage of it. Is it because the bank managers themselves are not telling the small businessmen that this assistance is available? The legislation needs a push along the line somewhere.
This government has to do even more than just amend the legislation. There used to be a department of government dealing with small businesses, but to my knowledge this department has been dissolved. If it is still functioning we certainly do not hear anything about it.
There is one other factor mentioned by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. The amount of the loan available is $25,000. That was the amount prescribed by the act when it was passed in 1961, but this is not nearly enough today. If a grocer wants to modernize his store and to instal modern refrigerating equipment to keep pace with large sales of frozen foods and other products requiring refrigeration today it will cost him $75,000, in order to compete and keep in line with his competitors. So that this amount of $25,000 is inadequate, and I am only sorry that the government did not see fit to raise
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment the amount and include this provision in its amendments to the act.
Many service businesses come within the act, but there is one that does not, one which is very important to the welfare of the country and to society as a whole. I am referring to professional men such as doctors and physiotherapists, osteopaths, dentists, etc. who want to start a practice, or a group of doctors who want to acquire a clinic and buy some of the very expensive equipment on the market today. This should be regarded as constituting a service business. These professional people need this help and should come within the ambit of the act, along with the other service businesses. If we were to look into this question further I am sure we would enlarge the terms of the act to include medical men, dentists, and so on, who could use a loan to great advantage. For example, I think of the young man who has just graduated and is starting up in practice. The provisions of this legislation would be a great help to him and would enable him to render services so badly needed in many of our communities.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I congratulate the government on broadening the scope of this excellent piece of legislation which we had the honour of introducing in 1961.

Mr. Chairman, I realize the wish of the committee to complete this resolution stage this evening. However, I wanted on behalf of this group to express our approval of the resolution, and to do so in a brief space of time.
I am well aware that small businesses provide two things which are becoming increasingly rare-personal service and neighbourhood convenience, two important items in today's world. We approve of the broadening of this act so as to extend its usefulness, but I should like to say that unless this parliament and the government do a few other things at the same time we may find, as often happens when small businesses are developed, that we are laying the groundwork for a national chain of some kind or other to take over. Often small businesses are sold rather swiftly, not because they do not make enough money but because of the frustrations of their owners as a result of government intervention.
I recall very vividly sitting down with a group of small businessmen at one time and asking them what was their main problem in this regard. There was a short pause, and then came the answer "Well, the government". I can think of a couple of examples. One is the requirement of making quarterly payments of income tax. When a small businessman just starting up business is asked to make quarterly payments of tax prior to the end of the year, with refusal to pay or tardiness in payment involving him in the payment of interest on money which I do not see how he can owe the government anyway, this puts him to some hardship. Another problem has been mentioned over and over again in this house and is created by the Canada Pension Plan, overpayments to which being not returnable to small businessmen. This is the kind of thing we should take care of at the same time as we take this forward step in broadening the terms of the act.

maintopic: RESEARCH-REQUEST FOR INCREASED GRANTS FOR MEDICAL RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I asked a question in the house about the possible loss of accreditation of four of Canada's 12 medical schools. I asked the question of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) because he had suggested that the rate of increase of the medical research council estimates be reduced. I understand that the rate has been allowed to go up again to the 30 per cent that had been allowed previously. In spite of this, I feel that the threat of the loss of accreditation of four of our medical schools is a disgrace to our country. At one time we had one of the best reputations in the world for medical science. What have we today? We have a government that fails to plan. As a result our country is on the verge of medical disaster.
The Financial Post has said this:
Canada's standard of health care is dangerously close to slipping quickly and quietly to the level of the second rate.
Our scientist medical teachers are going to the United States, where they have continuing money for the advancement of medical research. There, $6.50 per capita is spent, compared with Canada's 90 cents per capita.
Referring to a book put out as a report to the committee of presidents of the universities of Ontario entitled "Health Science in Ontario Universities", I see that it says on one page that teachers and scientists in
February 16, 1967	COMMONS
Canada must be encouraged to remain in academic work and Canadian teacher scientists and graduate students now employed in the United States must be attracted back to Canada if possible. On the next page, page 19, one sentence is worth repeating. It says that at the present time full-time staff will not join faculties of medicine lacking research facilities.
Now we are faced with the prospect of four additional new medical schools in Canada, one in Hamilton, at McMaster University. It is planned to open this in 1969. Prospective students for this are in pre-medical schools, at universities. They started last fall, in 1966. Why would a government commit itself to spending $500 million on health training facilities while not allowing for the payment of a staff of teacher-scientists to run these facilities?
We are still continuing to play musical chairs between the universities, rather than plan for the future and increase one of our most valuable commodities, the supply of medical teachers, by a proper government increase each year of 50 per cent, as requested as a minimum by the deans of our medical schools. The present rate is 30 per cent, a rate which was threatened last year by the Minister of Finance when he decided to cut back the rate of increase of these grants. His statement at that time undermined the morale of the teaching staffs at every medical university across this country, and did almost irreparable harm to the four newly formed medical schools.
In the past two or three days editorials have suggested that the government should spend the money set aside for medicare on medical research. This of course is ridiculous. But research should be a part of any complete medicare scheme. Members of this government have been seen by representatives of all the societies and associations of the medical profession and some of the most prominent and well-respected members of that profession have explained the situation, hoping to get a realistic amount of money, not for their own good but so that essential work might be carried on. But to no obvious avail.
Better planning and foresight on the part of the government would have resulted in a more realistic arrangement for looking after the health of the Canadian people. The research aspect is all part and parcel of the same deal. The government's attitude is comparable to organizing a public teaching system, and teaching only part of the curricula.

This government is encouraging private enterprise to do research for individual profit rather than for the benefit of the people of this country alone. The type of research which comes from private drug firms sets out to combine advantageously two or more well known drugs in a mixture which will bring a larger profit. Any worth while discoveries made in this or in other countries have been made by doctors doing university research. I might use insulin and penicillin, or even the sulphonamides as an example.
To my way of thinking, spending money along the lines I suggest would protect Canadians in at least two ways: it would keep the brains in Canada and it would allow the results of their research to be used to improve the health of Canadians and of others in the world, not solely for the profit of private enterprise. Mr. Speaker, on February 9 I put to the minister of Industry and of Defence Production the following question:
As a result of the trade mission to France and the report published in that connection, could the minister tell the house whether profitable relations and exchanges have been established between France and Canada regarding technical development and other joint projects?
Last year, a Canadian economic mission went to France with a view to promote closer relations between the two countries. A report has been published, and it would be interesting to know if practical results stemmed from those happy efforts.
From the standpoint of trade, the import-export picture between Canada and France represents a very small percentage, namely 1 per cent of all imports and exports between Canada and foreign countries. Our country would benefit very much by diversifying and increasing our commercial markets, particularly with a country like France who is a member of the European Common Market and in a position to export particular goods to our country in return for farm and manufactured products which abound here.
With respect to immigration in 1966, only 7,872 of a total 194,743 immigrants were of French nationality. There are various reasons for this small number of French immigrants. Canada should establish more immigration offices in France, we should invest more money in advertising programs and the R.C.M.P. should stop investigating each French immigrant, while immigrants from England and Ireland are accepted without any such formality.
French people should receive better assurance that they are most welcome in Canada and that skilled workmen will find here

DEBATES	February 16, 1967
immediately upon arrival permanent and remunerative work.
In the industrial field, direct exchanges of qualified personnel, the establishment of joint industrial research programs and other common projects should be undertaken, so that knowledge and skill would complement each other. Canada should also seriously consider adopting the metric system, in order better to follow the technical and industrial evolution and contend with the aggressive and perfected foreign production.
In the field of investments, Canada would greatly benefit from French capital, and the trade and economic development of both countries would gain a great deal by it.
Any effort by the central government to increase all types of relations with France would please all Canadians, I am sure, and especially the 7 million French Canadians. A bicultural country like Canada has the tremendous advantage of establishing more easily close and profitable relations with the French speaking world and Anglo-Saxon groups.

Mr. Speaker, the visit of the Canadian economic mission to France has clearly awakened interest in closer relations between the respective business communities.
Individual businessmen in both countries are responding to the encouragement by their respective governments that they seek to develop business with their counterparts. Among the initiatives which have been taken to follow up prospects, we know of Canadian companies which are pursuing particular opportunities with French firms, but we cannot divulge the nature of any of the negotiations now under way because of their private character.
To indicate the trend further, I can advise that we know of the intentions of groups of French businessmen from particular industries to visit Canada during our centennial year to explore trade prospects-in the aggregate a total of over 1,400 persons.
These increasing contacts will give rise to some technological exchange and probably joint ventures.
The full impact of the Canadian Mission will require time to reach and be seen in its full dimension.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for drawing this situation to my attention and commend him for his ever-vigilant interest in farmers' affairs, and particularly those affecting his own constituency. With respect to the stabilization payments, the deficiency payments, I think the hon. member will agree that we can at the federal level have only a national basis of deficiency payments. If we were to have regional deficiency payments we would but contribute to the fragmentation, economically, of the nation. Any program we have must be a national one.
I would point out to the hon. member that some provinces have provincial egg marketing boards which work in conjunction with our federal stabilization program and deficiency program, to achieve possibly a more perfect equity for farmers in those provinces. I personally am a believer in the system invoked by the National Dairy Commission, and I think under our constitutional concept the best set-up one can conceive in agriculture is provincial boards that work in conjunction and co-operation with a national board, so that both intraprovincial and extraprovincial marketing can be covered by these two entities within their proper jurisdictional authority.

It is my hope that in the not too distant future there will be a national egg marketing board of the same type and nature as the National Dairy Commission, and that this board can work in conjunction with similar provincial boards to achieve a greater stability in egg marketing and egg pricing and, I think, thus ensure greater justice for our egg producers.
I might point out that there certainly has been a drop in price in the past few weeks, but that during the past year egg prices have been much better than they have been over the past number of years. This of course encouraged increased production. Irrespective of general price trends during any production

year there is always an increase of deliveries during mid-January and we always experience a drop in prices at that time. This year the mid-January problem has persisted over the past four weeks because of the current supply-demand picture. Present indications are that production is dropping off and it is expected that when the supply is more in line with demand, prices will become more firm. I can assure the hon. member that the Agricultural Stabilization Board is keeping this situation under constant review.
